comments.author: tpoacher
comments.story_title: The hidden cost of AI coding
comments.why_zh: 把60年代的烤面包机当作优雅旧技术的一份惊喜。
comments.quote_zh: 如果你还没看过这个60年代烤面包机的视频，那你有福了
comments.text_zh: 一个相关的想法，就随手放在这儿。旧技术身上确实有很棒的东西（虽然引用这类技术时显然得注意幸存者偏差），尽管从逻辑上讲，新技术本来显然应该更好。也许这是杰文斯悖论的某种变体。东西越好、越高效，就越有动力把它们用在真正糟糕的用途上。而我开始对“用 AI 编程 vs 不用 AI 编程”有这种感觉：你要么手工编程，做出真正有创意、能干活、优雅的东西，要么用 AI 更高效地生产垃圾。似乎就是没有中间地带，至少从需求上看是这样。如果你还没看过这个60年代烤面包机的视频，那你有福了：[VIDEO] 这也让我想起 Edsger Dijkstra 关于优雅的那句话：[LINK]
comments.text: A related thought, just leaving this here. There's something great about old technology (though obviously one must be aware of survivorship bias when citing such technology), despite the fact that, logically speaking, new technology should have obviously been better. Perhaps it's some variant of Jevons' paradox. The better / more efficient things get, the more of an impetus there is to use them in truly crappy ways. And this is how I'm starting to feel about programming with vs without an AI: you can either program manually to create truly creative, functional, elegant stuff, or use AI to produce garbage more efficiently. There just doesn't seem to be an in-between category, at least in terms of demand. In case you haven't seen this video of a toaster from the 60s before, you're in for a treat: [VIDEO] I'm also reminded of Edsger Dijkstra's quote on elegance: [LINK]

comments.why_zh: 另一件没有微控制器、设计优雅的机械奇迹。
comments.quote_zh: 我觉得这个19分钟的视频值得一看
comments.text_zh: > 你可能会以为这样的系统得有恒温器、微控制器和执行器，但这个设计 [...] 用的是双金属臂，外表面是钢，内表面是铜。随着灯丝加热，金属臂升温，铜的膨胀比钢快。这种膨胀把金属臂撑开，释放点烟器。接着螺旋弹簧让手柄弹出，表示点烟器已经就绪。也许我今天有点挑剔，但在我看来，引言写得好像这三样东西（恒温器、微控制器、执行器）都不必要，可实际上这个设计里缺的只有微处理器（恒温器→双金属臂，执行器→弹簧）。照例附上同一问题领域里另一件神奇之作的链接（我觉得这个19分钟的视频值得一看）：“An Antique Toaster That's Better Than Today’s [video]” [VIDEO] [LINK] [2019, 386 points|5 years ago|232 comments]
comments.text: > You might think such a system would involve a thermostat, a microcontroller, and an actuator, but this design [...] has bimetallic arms with steel on the outer surface and copper on the inner surface. As the filament heats up, the arms warm up, causing the copper to expand faster than the steel. This expansion pushes the arms open, releasing the lighter. The coil spring then causes the handle to pop out, signaling that the lighter is ready. Maybe I am in a picky mood, but for me the intro made it sound like all three items (thermostat, microcontroller, actuator) would not be necessary, though of course only the microprocessor is missing from the design (thermostat -> bimetallic arms, actuator -> spring). Mandatory link to another marvel in the same problem space (I found the 19min video worth the time): "An Antique Toaster That's Better Than Today’s [video]" [VIDEO] [LINK] [2019, 386 points|5 years ago|232 comments]
